dialog.body: Zoning and Inspections, this is Anita. How can I help you?
Hi, yes, good afternoon. My name is Omar Cohen. I'm calling about a fence. I want to put up a fence, and I'm not sure what the rules are.
Okay, sure, I can help with that. Can I get the address where the fence would go?
It's 246 Narragansett Avenue. That's in the Fifth Ward, I believe. Is that what they call it?
Yes, that's right, Fifth Ward. And what kind of fence are you thinking about, and what's it for?
So, it's for the garden. I have a vegetable garden in the back, and the deer come through at night and eat everything. The tomatoes, the beans, all of it. I want a fence to keep the deer out.
Got it. Deer can be tough. Do you know yet what material you want?
Vinyl. I want vinyl, because wood, you have to paint it, and I'm done with painting. And I want it tall. Whatever is allowed tall. Deer jump, you know, so the fence has to be high.
Right, they can clear a fairly low fence. So the height is something I'd want to look at for you. Is this around the whole yard, or just around the garden area?

Just the garden. Well, um, the garden is in the back corner, so it would run along the side, near the neighbor. Part of it, anyway. So is that the whole yard or the garden? I guess it's both, sort of.
Okay, so part of it might run along the side of your property. That matters. Let me ask your main question first, though. What did you want to know?

Yes. Do I need to pull a permit before the guy starts? The fence guy. He says he can start in a couple weeks, and he said something about a permit, but I thought the permit was only for a building. A house. Not a fence.
Generally, a fence does need a permit here, yes. It's not only for buildings. So you'd want to have that squared away before the installer puts anything in the ground.
Oh. So the fence needs a permit. Even a garden fence. Even if it's small, like a garden fence?

A garden fence that's tall enough to keep deer out is going to be a regular fence as far as we're concerned, so I'd plan on needing one. Does your installer usually handle the application, or are you doing it yourself?
I don't know. He said, you pull the permit, I think. Or maybe he pulls it. Honestly, I wasn't listening so good. I'll ask him. He's a nice fellow but he talks fast.
That's fine, ask him which it is. Either way, the application is made with the property owner's information, so you'll be involved.
Okay. And then the other thing. How close to the property line is allowed? Can I put it right on the line? Because the neighbor has a hedge, and I don't want a fight about the hedge.

There are usually setback rules for how far in from the line a fence has to sit, and they can depend on the height and the zone. I don't want to give you a number that's wrong for your lot. Do you have a survey or a plot plan of the property?
A survey. Hmm. I have some papers from when I bought the house. There's a drawing, with lines. Is that the survey?
It might be. If it shows the lot lines and the house measurements, that's what you want. Look for a stamp or a surveyor's name on it. That will help show where your line actually is.

Okay, I'll look. I'm in the kitchen right now, the papers are upstairs. And I can't go up right now, because I'm babysitting my grandson for the afternoon. He's finally quiet, and I'm not touching anything.

Understood, don't wake the peace. You don't have to do it right now. Here's what I'd suggest. Find that drawing, talk to your installer about who files, and then you can come in or call back with the details and we can go over the height and the distance from the line.
So, the height. You can't tell me the height now? The tall one I want?

I can't give you a firm number on the phone, because it can change depending on where the fence sits, front yard or back, and the zone. For a back garden it's often more flexible than the front. But I'd rather you hear the exact figure from the permit review.
Okay. So, back is more flexible. But the permit is needed. And the line, I need the survey. Did I get that right?
You did. Permit first, before the installer starts. Survey or plot plan to check the line. And the height gets confirmed when you apply.
Good. And do I come there, to City Hall, for the application? Or is there a form I can get?
You can come to our office, and I can hand you the form. Or I can have someone go over the steps with you if you call back. Would you like me to note your number in case we need to reach you?
Got it, 401-555-0172, Omar Cohen, 246 Narragansett Avenue, fence question. I'll put that in the notes.
Thank you. I think I understand. Mostly. I'll tell the fence guy to wait on the permit.
That's the right idea. Have a good weekend, Mr. Cohen.
You too. Thank you, bye now.
